en: Recorded Discourse on the Entrance into the Inner Quarters and the Ascending of the Seat by Wuzu Heshang of Jingshan;
compiled by Attendants Liaonan and Liaoyin on the fifteenth day of the seventh month in the sixth year of the Shaoding era.

The Emperor, presiding in the Xiuzheng Hall, received the Master and the assembly of monks from his temple led by Shan Shou. Zhang Yanqing, the Grand Marshal and Director of the Bureau of Supervision, introduced them as they offered prayers for the Emperor’s longevity.

The Master held up the incense and said: "Its roots are one with Heaven and Earth; its excellence emerges from the mountains and rivers. It wafts and mingles in the precious burner, a auspicious sign..."

Leaping across the realms of dust, I respectfully offer congratulations on the Emperor’s Divine Person, praying for ten thousand years, ten thousand years, ten thousand times ten thousand years! Pointing to the Seven Golden Mountains, I designate them as the Mountain of Longevity.

Majestic and immovable, he takes the four great oceans as his sea of merit; vast and boundless, he eternally dwells as the Honored One of the Northern Pole and forever serves as the Sovereign of the Central Heaven.
With golden branches and jade leaves, he nurtures excellence and spreads fragrance; the eight quarters submit to his benevolence, and the myriad states present their tribute.
The Grand Marshal Du Zhi said, "I beg the Elder to expound upon this. Thereupon he addressed the assembly, saying: "I, the monk Shifan..."
I am but a single, humble monk born in Western Sichuan. Having wandered across lakes and seas for forty years now, I have heard nothing of the Way and feel constant self-reproach.

By what good fortune in past lives have I twice received Your Majesty’s gracious decree, first to sweep and purify Qingyuan Yuyang and then to reach Shuangjing. Since taking office last August, I have...

The monastics from the four quarters have been engaged in meditation and recitation morning and evening to offer their reverent gratitude for the sagely grace of the Emperor. Unforeseen, however, on the night of the twenty-first day of the fourth month, they were suddenly struck by fire.
Yet, fortune and misfortune cannot escape the decree of destiny; this was truly brought about by the meager merit of this humble monk. He immediately proceeded to...
The court prostrates itself to await punishment.
By Your Majesty’s vast benevolence, you have not yet deigned to execute us.
Immediately thereafter, we were granted an imperial decree bestowing one hundred *duodie* certificates. Once again, we are indebted for this grace.
By imperial grace, fifty additional ordination certificates were specially bestowed, and the temple was ordered to be rebuilt from the foundations.
This bounty is as vast as heaven, leaving us ignorant of how to repay it.
We reflect deeply that our mountain monastery is a place where Emperor Gaozong once visited in person.
This is the foremost site for the imperial court’s prayers. The construction of this temple complex is truly difficult to complete within the allotted time;
we can only rely upon Your Majesty’s sacred grace to ensure its early completion, for which we are most profoundly grateful. In the past, even the Jetavana Vihāra suffered from such calamities.
The Vinaya Master Tang Yi once asked the Venerable Deva Vaiśravaṇa:

"When the World-Honored One, whose merit is an immeasurable ocean, preaches the Dharma, all the Buddhas of the ten directions, the great Bodhisattvas, and the devas, nāgas, and spirits assemble there;
this is called a ground of auspiciousness and a most excellent place. How could such a calamity as this occur? The Deva Vaiśravaṇa replied: "This is the Southern Heaven..."
The Celestial King, by the power of his great vows, shall rebuild this temple; therefore, he has burned it down.

Now that Your Majesty has bestowed such gracious favors and is restoring Mount Jing, is this not because Your Majesty’s vast and sagely mind is equal, without distinction, to the vow-power of the Southern Heavenly King? Thus, this broad...
The Great Mind is never separate from daily life; it moves with ease through the myriad functions of the world.

It distinguishes the heterodox from the orthodox and discerns right from wrong without the slightest concealment, like a bright mirror set upon its stand that reflects whatever comes before it. There is not a single dharma that does not manifest from the mind.
If Your Majesty preserves this mind to sustain the world, the world will be entirely submissive.
If you expand this mind to transform the myriad states, the myriad states will come to court. If you extend this mind to honor the Buddha-dharma, the Buddha-dharma will flourish.

If you purify this mind to practice benevolence and filial piety, benevolence and filial piety will reach their ultimate fulfillment. This humble monk offers these words like a rustic man presenting his wild vegetable; such is what I have set forth.
My words are beyond compare;
I have presumed upon Your Majesty’s sagacious hearing. My humble feelings are overcome with the utmost trepidation and perspiration.
I immediately received the Imperial decree bestowing the golden-embroidered *kāṣāya*. [I] thank [you].
The expression of gratitude concluded. The Emperor again granted the assembly of monks seats for the communal meal.
When the meal was finished, they once more expressed their thanks and descended from the hall.
At noon, he was proclaimed to proceed to the Shrine of the Imperial Highness, Empress Dowager Gongsheng Renlie, and ascend the throne.
The Emperor presides behind the curtain. The Master ascends the seat and holds up the incense, saying: "Flowing forth from within the ocean of samādhi, it is neither wood nor smoke;
bestowed from the Nine Palaces above the heavens, it is most honored and most precious.
I reverently offer this for the supreme benefit of the Empress Dowager Gongsheng Renshu."
"Immortal Chariot! I humbly pray that you may roam and wander through the three thousand golden worlds of the Buddha-lands, and dwell and reside within the twelve jade towers of the Immortals' abode.
Having taken his seat, he spoke these words: "The essential intent of Vulture Peak; the true wind of Shaoshi."
Before a single word was uttered, the four seas were set in motion. Is there anyone who can stir this up together?

At that time, a monk stepped forth from the assembly and said, "I do not know how deep the great ocean is; I shall simply cast my silk line down once to probe it. The Master said, "Look beneath your feet.
The monk asked, "In years past, you descended to the Jade Pond under the moon to serve as a model of motherhood for the human world. After the banquet at Guang..."
"The way back from the cold is secure; to this day, his profound virtue spreads throughout the realm of Kun. At such a time as this, I wish to hear his proclamation.
He replied, "The entire great chiliocosm is moistened by his grace. The questioner continued, "All classes of beings, including devas and humans, receive this power of grace."
The answer was: "Where there is water, it contains the moon; where there is no mountain, it does not bear clouds. The questioner pressed further:
"I recall that when the King of the Western Heaven (India) learned his mother had ascended to the realm of immortals, he wept with sorrow and said to the Buddha:

'If my mother's life could be extended, I would offer all things in this world to prolong it. What is the meaning of this? The answer was: "Relinquish everything throughout your entire being; touch [the truth]."
Seeing the Compassionate Countenance, he stepped forward and said, “The World-Honored One has preached the subtle and supreme Dharma; how, then, is this subtle and supreme Dharma preached?
He replied, “Mountains, rivers, and the great earth radiate light. He asked further, “When the King rejoices, receives it upon his head, and puts it into practice, what then?
He replied, “It requires a person of extraordinary capacity to clarify matters of extraordinary scope. He asked again, “Just so...”

[The questioner said: "Just as the Upādhyāya has today been commanded to propagate the teachings and the tradition, how does this differ from the past? [The Master] replied: "All the stars bow toward the North;
the ten thousand streams all flow toward the source. [The questioner] continued: "If that is so, then I..."
The Empress Dowager did not need to move her fingers; she turned and became a Buddha. He replied, "True nature is naturally golden bone;
there is no need for sandalwood to be finely carved. He pressed further, "I have already received the Master’s instruction on the news;
as for the ultimate vehicle of the ancestral school, what is it like? He replied, "Everyone looks up with their faces raised. He pressed further.
Emperor Xiaozong asked Chan Master Fozhao, "What was it that the World-Honored One accomplished during his six years in the Snowy Mountains?
What was Your Majesty’s intention? The Emperor replied, "The words of a king are like a single strand of silk; once they issue forth, they become a thick cord.
Fozhao answered, "I had thought..."
[The Emperor] said, "Your Majesty has forgotten. Is it not truly so? He replied, "The Snowy Mountains cast their lofty reflection upon the Golden Hall.
[The Emperor] asked, "Why was Zen Master Fo-zhao, great or small as he may have been, reduced to vomiting forth his entire heart when faced with this single question?

He replied, "In the presence of a sagely sovereign, how could one permit concealment or evasion? [The Emperor] asked, "In the past, the auspicious assembly of ruler and subject—how was this any different from [the present]?"
"The dragon obtains the water; the tiger relies on the mountain. He replied, "A model for all time, past and present. The student asked, "Today is a meeting of a thousand-year cycle;
it may be said that the moon is reflected in the clear pool, and the wind rises through ten thousand ravines. He replied, "This story has already spread throughout the world."
The student said, "At this very moment, how do you express a word of gratitude? The Master replied, "The sea is vast and the mountains are high;
it is not easy to speak of. The student said, "A monk beneath the forest trees has no means to repay [your kindness], relying only on a single incense burner morning and evening."
The Master replied, "One must simply act thus. Another monk stepped forward and asked, "In the Hall of the Funeral Rites, the precious torches are lit;
flowers and incense scatter through the nine heavens. We pray to hear the essential Dharma. The Master replied, "Upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, the golden bell is struck.
The monk pressed further, "If that is so, then today we have heard what was never heard before. The Master replied, "All are invited to realize perfect penetration. The monk pressed further.

[Question: "I recall how the World-Honored One held up a flower and Kāśyapa smiled. What is the principle behind this? [Answer: "When the mud-bull bellows, the mountains and rivers are still; when the wooden horse neighs, the sun and moon shine bright.

[Question (Jin):**] "Dīpaṃkara personally inherited the Patriarchal seat, and Bodhidharma directly pointed to the human mind. It has been transmitted for over two thousand years; I wonder what it is that has been transmitted? [Answer: "The entire nation... *Note:

The text provided ends abruptly with "闔國" (the whole country). Based on the context of classical Chan/Zen dialogues, the expected response would likely continue with a phrase such as "闔國盡是箇箇丈夫" (The entire nation is entirely composed of great men), indicating that the truth is universal and inherent.*
Everyone knew this. [Zhao] Jin said, "If that is so, then for the first time I believe that matters from the distant *Pǔtōng* era were not brought over from the Pamir Mountains.
The Master replied, "My hazy eyes have opened; the neighbor’s rooster has already crowed three times. Jin said, "As for today, how does the Master respectfully serve [the Emperor]?"
Regarding the posthumous honors bestowed upon the Empress Dowager, what Dharma was proclaimed to uplift her?
The Master held up his whisk and said, "Relying solely on this true message, she is offered to the blissful heavens of the immortal journey.

A monk stepped forward and asked, "I recall the Empress Dowager praising the Great Being Avalokiteśvara, saying: 'The Great Being possesses the marks of meditative concentration; his manifestations are immeasurable. What did he do?"
"What is the meditative mark of the Great Being? He replied, "It cannot be traced; it cannot be painted. [The questioner] pressed further:

"The pure contemplation throughout the kalpas brings swift peace and security to devas and humans. What is this state of peace and security? He replied, "In every atom there is neither facing nor turning away;
in every thought-moment it is inconceivable. [The questioner] pressed further: "Even when manifesting illusory forms, one accords with the Suchness of the fundamental."
[Question: "Is the illusory image and the original reality one or two? [Answer: "The Southern Tiantai and the Northern Wutai.
[Follow-up Question: "Potalaka is supramundane. If a person pays homage with reverence, what is this supramundane matter? [Answer: "..."
"Not departing from the marks of the world. [The Master] continued, "This single verse of praise alone transcends past and present;
it is shared equally by the Great Being Avalokiteśvara.
Furthermore, in which land does the Empress Dowager currently reside? He replied, "In the place where the nine lotuses open and close, the hundred jewels adorn themselves naturally."
Yan asked, "Do you permit a student of the Way to speak of the place where all Buddhas emerge? He replied, "Today, right before your eyes, it is precisely the time to bring it forth.
Yan said, "The nine heavens are clear and the myriad sounds are hushed; the single moon is reflected in a thousand rivers. He replied, "Indeed."
"What wonderful news! Another monk stepped forward and asked: 'Last night a rain fell that moistened heaven and earth, fully revealing the gate of non-dual Suchness.
Now the Dharma assembly in the imperial garden has been grandly inaugurated; the gathering on Vulture Peak remains as if present. At this very moment, we pray the Master [will speak].'"
The Master raised the topic. The disciple replied, “The bright sun is at its zenith; the fragrant breeze pervades the earth.

The Master pressed further, “If that is so, then the Phoenix Hall and Dragon Tower abound with auspicious qi, and the Golden Steps and Jade Palace are enveloped in radiant light. The Master replied, “Truly a magnificent world. The disciple then asked:
[The Master] recalled: "When Śakra rained down flowers while Subhūti was sitting in meditative seclusion within the cave, what did he say?

[The disciple] replied: "The horse's head leans toward the wealthy gate. [The Master] pressed: "How could Śakra have caused the rain of flowers? I saw the Venerable One skillfully expound the Prajñāpāramitā—how about that?
He replied: "Chewing frost and ice with a full mouth. [The Master] pressed: "High mountains and flowing water—the one who knows the music."
"Listen. 'Leaves falling, one knows autumn'—this is something those who are proficient understand. He replied, "Bo Ya and Zi Qi were not merely acquaintances.
He further asked, "Subhūti said, 'I have never spoken a single word regarding Prajñāpāramitā. Ultimately, was it speaking?"
“Do you not speak? He replied, “My tongue supports the Brahma-heaven. The questioner pressed further, “Śakra said, ‘Venerable sir, you have nothing to say;
I, too, have nothing to hear. This is called the true preaching of Prajñāpāramitā. How is this principle to be understood? He replied, “When the benevolent see it, they call it benevolence;
when the wise see it, they call it wisdom. The questioner continued, “Today the Master respectfully faces the funeral altar to proclaim [the Dharma].”

"Regarding Prajñā: [it is used] for the posthumous offering for the Empress Dowager’s ascent to the immortal realm. Is what was spoken by Subhūti the same as this, or is it different? He replied, "Sanskrit is the language of the Western Heaven;
Chinese is the speech of this land. He further asked, "To solemnly honor the Empress Dowager’s transcendence beyond the Three Realms, I look up and offer these prayers."
"May the imperial domain endure for ten million years. He replied, "So it is; so it is. The Master said:
"The source of the Great Way, the mother of the myriad things—empty space cannot match its vastness, and the blue seas are insufficient to compare with its depth.

It can illuminate the brilliance of the sun and moon and augment the stability of the mountains and rivers. Its measure encompasses all goodness, its vital energy sustains all spirits, and its virtue spreads throughout the world."

The universe is like springtime amidst a hundred flowers; his brilliant assistance at the pivot of government is like a mirror facing ten thousand images. When a cycle of affairs is completed, he does not abide by old conventions;
attaining a body born of mastery, he moves spontaneously according to circumstances. At such a time as this—
"Respectfully addressing the Empress Dowager Gongsheng Renshile: Where have you gone? The troupe of immortals stirs to the sound of music;

colorful clouds swirl around the palace of the Buddha. (Your servant), the monk Shifan, has just been graced by Your Majesty’s radiant presence, honored with the gift of a golden robe, and further favored with a meal. I am deeply moved by this grace."
Your Sacred Grace: I am utterly unable to repay Your bounty.

Now, having once again received Your Imperial Decree, I shall reverently ascend the seat before the funerary altar of the Empress Dowager to proclaim the Tathāgata’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the Wondrous Mind of Nirvāṇa. I prostrate myself.

It is by the grace of Your Majesty that, for the sake of the Buddha-dharma, Your Sacred Person has deigned to descend. However, I, the monk Shifan, am rustic and unrefined, and my speech is coarse and uncultivated; I fear I have been too presumptuous.
"Your Sacred Majesty, I beg leave to prostrate myself and offer my apologies once these matters are concluded. However, this sequence of events is truly rare.
In the past we heard of the supreme filial piety of the Great Shun; now we behold Your Majesty’s ability to practice it.

Were it not for having deeply grasped the mind of the Sage and simultaneously realized the subtlety of the Buddha-vehicle, how could one have reached such a state? Since antiquity, emperors and kings have devoted their attention to this Way."
Such instances are not limited to one; I dare not cite them all in detail.
For example, during the reign of Emperor Daizong of the Tang dynasty, he also once summoned the founding patriarch Guoyi of Mount Wutai and treated him with constant reverence and respect.
Once, encountering cold weather, Daizong covered the master’s head with a dragon-sleeved robe made of gold-threaded silk. Later, the master eventually used that dragon-sleeved robe as a cap. Until...
Now, the portrait of the Patriarch remains solemnly preserved even today.
Furthermore, Emperor Taizong of our sagely dynasty had a profound realization of the essence of the Buddha-dharma. One day, while visiting Daxiangguo Monastery, he saw a monk reading a sutra.
The Emperor asked, "What sutra are you reading? The monk replied, "The *Benevolent Kings Sutra for Protecting the State*. The Emperor said, "Since it is..."
"Your humble servant’s sutra has, for some reason, ended up in your hands, Your Excellency. The monk remained silent.
Later, Chan Master Fohai spoke on his behalf, holding the sutra scroll as if grasping a ceremonial tablet and saying: "May the Emperor enjoy ten thousand blessings."
The Emperor Zhenzong once composed a verse on the meaning of the Westward Transmission, saying: "The First Patriarch sat in meditation at Shaolin;

He did not transmit the Dharma-teachings, but transmitted only the mind. If later people wish to awaken to the nature of True Suchness, They must know that the wondrous intent of the secret seal has always been profound.
Were it not for one who clearly penetrates the school beyond the teachings, How could this be easily attained?"

Emperor Renzong once summoned Chan Master Dajue Liai to ascend the seat; the exchange between sovereign and subject has remained celebrated to this day, with the Imperial Calligraphy at Yuyang Temple still resplendent.
Emperors Yingzong, Shenzong, and Zhezong all likewise summoned Chan Master Jingzhao and Chan Master Foguo to the Longevity [Monastery].
He ascended the seat at the Qingdian, Funingdian, and Cidehuan halls; this has been fully recorded in the *Xùdēng* (Continued Lamp Records).
Emperor Gaozong also summoned Chan Master Yuanwu to ascend the seat, for which there is a verse that says: "Cultivated by one of great merit and virtue."

Those of great merit receive [the fruits of their deeds]; good causes invite good results. Just as sowing grain does not produce beans, though these words may be plain and rustic, they are nonetheless direct.
Emperor Xiaozong especially struck his palm in approval at the Zen barrier;
he frequently summoned more than ten masters from various mountains, such as Chan Master Fohai, Biefeng, Mian, Shui’an, Zide, and others—all of whom were honored by him.
The Imperial Consort. Zen Master Fozhao was staying at Guantang for five nights. He once said to Fozhao, "My mind and the Buddha-mind are in communication.
Fozhao replied, "Right here, there is no second person. The Emperor said, "Since ancient times, there have been many heroic emperors and kings, but few who have truly believed in this Way;
even Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty had not yet reached full penetration. Fozhao submitted in response: "When..."

To have missed the opportunity to encounter Bodhidharma face-to-face— where the dialogue between sovereign and subject resounded like the chime of gold and jade— is truly something rarely heard since antiquity.
We look up to Your Majesty,
who takes the Buddha-dharma as your heart’s core and practices benevolence and filial piety as the basis of your governance.
Your Majesty is divinely gifted and has attained profound mastery of the ultimate truth; thus, the ministers of this era are all like Gao Yao, Kui, Ji, and Xie.
You honor the Three Teachings equally, such that even the grasses, trees, insects, and creatures all receive your benevolent grace.
(I, your subject) the monk Gu, though not daring to hope to equal my predecessors, nevertheless strive to set forth my humble views to respectfully uphold [your legacy].
Your Majesty’s intention of pure filial piety—that which was previously called the Tathāgata’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the Wondrous Mind of Nirvāṇa—is none other than this very mind.
It is the mind possessed by every person; from the sovereign above down to the common people below, there are none who do not fully possess this mind.
Therefore, when Śākyamuni Buddha was once on the Snowy Mountains, he suddenly beheld the morning star at night.
Upon attaining this realization, he sighed, saying: "How marvelous! How marvelous! All sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtues, and marks of a Tathāgata;

yet, because of deluded thoughts and attachments, they are unable to realize them. During the twenty-one days [following his enlightenment], he contemplated these matters, finding no words with which to express them.
He then recalled the power of the skillful means practiced by the Buddhas of the past, and thereupon rose from beneath the Bodhi tree.
He went to the Deer Park and preached the twelve divisions of the teachings of the Three Vehicles, filling the dragon palaces and overflowing the ocean treasuries.

Seeing that the faculties and capacities of the assembly had matured, he finally, before a multitude of one million people, held up a single flower and gazed at the great assembly with his blue-lotus eyes.
The entire assembly remained silent; only Kāśyapa broke into a smile. The World-Honored One said: "I have..."
The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa, was entrusted to Mahākāśyapa. Thereafter, Kāśyapa transmitted it to Ānanda;
Ānanda transmitted it to Śāṇakavāsin, continuing down through the twenty-eight patriarchs of India and the six patriarchs of this land.
Subsequently, it divided into two schools and branched into five lineages, all of which transmitted mind by mind like water merging with water. Until—
To manifest the great capacity for awakening and display the great function, there emerges a wondrousness that transcends all schools and surpasses all categories.

It unties the adhesions and removes the fetters of all people, extracts the wedges and pulls out the nails, causing every person to clarify their own mind and perceive their own nature, proceeding directly to the ground of peace and bliss.
Yet this mind is able to establish all dharmas; there is not a single dharma that does not arise from the mind’s establishment.
"What person can go out without passing through the door? Why is it that no one follows this path? This path cannot be abandoned for even a moment;
that which can be abandoned is not the Way. As for "encountering the source at every turn," what else could it be?

Nevertheless, the sages of the Three Teachings share the same tongue, yet each has opened their own gate. When one investigates their ultimate aim, there is not the slightest difference between them. Only...
The Chan school is a separate transmission outside the teachings. It transcends the realm of words, phrases, feelings, and consciousness;
it is called the gateless gate. One must find this gate and enter. If one truly succeeds in entering the gateless gate, then the entire earth is not anything other than a gate.
Only then can one freely enter and exit, roll up and unroll, attaining great mastery. Simply take what has been raised and proclaimed above...
A single word, a single question and answer—these accord with the Buddhas and the Patriarchs, and accord with the holy and the mundane.

With these merits, I respectfully offer them to assist the Imperial Grandmother, the Most Virtuous and Benevolent Empress Dowager, in her ascension to the realm of the immortals. Looking up in reverence, I consider...

The Empress Dowager first resided in the central hall and subsequently attended the Eastern Court. She held profound faith in the Buddha-vehicle and attained deep realization of its doctrines and principles.
Her divine faculties operated with singular mastery, and her wisdom-nature was perfectly luminous. Having manifested the dignity of a mother, she shall now ascend to the stage of fruition.

We humbly pray that she may ride upon celestial music to soar into the Tuṣita Heaven, and that as golden lotuses support her feet, she may immediately realize Bodhi. May she further radiate her compassionate light to protect [the realm].
May it protect the state and its people.

We respectfully pray that Your Majesty, the Emperor, may see the mountain of your longevity grow ever steeper and the ocean of your blessings deepen ever further; that you may abide in vast non-action, and that the common people may transform themselves spontaneously.
I pray that for the Empress, the Imperial Consorts, and all the members of the imperial household, a thousand auspicious signs may converge and ten thousand virtues may arrive.
May a worthy heir be nurtured, further strengthening the foundation of the state. This servant-monk, having exhausted his sincere devotion, shall further recount one more causal narrative.

I recall that when Emperor Shenzong [Shenzong] was observing a fast for the late Empress Dowager Cisheng Guangxian at the Qingshou Hall, he invited Chan Master Jingzhao of the Shifang Jinyuan Monastery to ascend the seat and preach. At that time, a monk asked: "The Great..."
The Immortal has since departed on his travels; where is he now? Chan Master Jingzhao said: "When the moon sets, it does not leave the sky.
(I, the monk,) borrowing water to offer flowers, have ventured to compose this verse: Before sound, the phrase is attained, encompassing heaven and earth;

Vividly impartial, its wondrousness leaves no trace. The azure void, polished like bronze, reveals the autumnal colors; The cassia orb, lofty and pure, abides forever. I beg your indulgence for this intrusion.
"O Sage of Sagacity! Your humble servant’s feelings are beyond measure, filled with the utmost urgency and trepidation. [The monk] descended from his seat.
The Emperor was greatly pleased and bestowed upon him generous gifts. He then expressed his gratitude and descended from the hall.
The Record of the Ascension of the Throne and the Discourses of Wuzu Heshang of Jingshan (End).
A Biographical Account of Chan Master Wuzu of Jingshan,
composed by Can Wuwen.
The Master’s name was Shifan; his style name was Wuzhun. He was born into the Yong clan in Zizhong, Shu. At the age of nine, he entered the monastic life under the monk Daoqin at Mount Yinping.
Upon merely glancing over the scriptures and books, he could recite them from memory. Furthermore, he took delight in reading the essential sayings of the Chan school.
The elder brother, Cheng Dao Yin, was renowned for his lectures. He would frequently test the Master with probing questions regarding karmic conditions (*jīyuán*).

The Master responded to them as surely as an echo. Once, while they were reciting a sutra, he suddenly asked, "What sutra are you looking at? The Master held up the scroll and said, "A sutra such as this. Dao Yin was left bewildered.
One day, the Master questioned Dao Yin on the story of the woman in *dìng* (the fixed state). Dao Yin attempted to explain it using doctrinal interpretations. The Master laughed.
Thus it was. In the tenth month of the fifth year of the Shaohui era, he received full ordination. He then intended to travel south to seek instruction, but his mother, Lady He, fell gravely ill.
The Master cut flesh from his own thigh to provide medicine for her recovery. The following year, he arrived in Chengdu and spent the summer retreat at Zhengfa Temple.

The Head Seat there was Old Yao, a senior disciple of Xiatang whose spiritual practice was renowned throughout Sichuan. The Master requested instruction on the method of sitting meditation. Yao asked, "What is this thing called 'Chan'? Why sit?"
"Who is this? The Master accepted these words and investigated them day and night. One day, while at the toilet, he brought up the previous dialogue and attained realization.
In the autumn of the sixth year, he went next to Yuyuan Temple in Jingnan. There was an elder named Lao Su who had formerly studied under Dahui;

when the elder saw that Liaozhou had reached the depths [of understanding], the Master moved between these two elders and gained much from their discourse and essential instructions. The following year...
He took his leave and visited Baoning Quanwuyong and Jingshan Qitaian. Taian asked, "For what purpose have you come from so far?
The Master replied, "To investigate and clarify my own fundamental matter. Taian asked, "When birth and death arrive, what then?
The Master replied, "It has neither birth nor death. Taian said, "Go to the meditation hall. After some time, he traveled to Siming and relied upon Rui Xiuyan of Yuwang.
At that time, Chan Master Shaozhi resided at Dong’an (East Hermitage), with the elder Yin Kong serving as his seat-mate.

The assembly at the Dharma seat was so magnificent that it was considered the foremost in the southeastern region. Among those present were Jue Wuxiang, Kang Taiping, Yuan Qing’ou, Yan Zhe’ou, Quan Guyun, and Song Shaolin.
There was also the senior seat-holder Laoshen, a native of Sichuan who had been ill for a long time; the Master attended to him.
[He] attended to [Deshen’s] medicinal decoctions. Deshen had always maintained that "a single shout" was his primary practice.

When Fozhao went to inquire after his illness, he said to Deshen, "Head Seat Deshen, why do you not let out a shout? Deshen instead let out a shout. Fozhao said, "You still maintain a sense of self-mastery.
He then turned to the Master (Wuzu Fayan) and asked, "Where are you from? The Master replied, "From Jianzhou. Fozhao asked, "Did you bring your sword with you? The Master followed [his gaze].
Sheng shouted, and Fozhao laughed, saying, "This fellow with the black head is acting recklessly. The Master was only twenty years old, yet his composure in the face of such challenges was like this.
He was extremely poor and lacked the funds to shave his hair; thus, Fozhao often referred to him in his quarters as "the black-headed one.
Kong Sou once pointed to the Master and said to the assembly, "Fan is only twenty years old; in two more years..."
Ten years passed before his progress could be measured. Subsequently, he crossed the Qiantang River and met Master Yue Songyuan at Lingyin Temple.

He traveled back and forth to Nanshan, frequently entering the quarters of Master Chen Ken tang. He resided on this mountain for six years. Later, while traveling to Wumen, he visited Master Wu Zhen at Wanshou Temple.
At that time, the late Master Po’an was residing at Xihu Xiufeng; he went there to rely upon him, where there were more than ten monks in the hall.

These individuals were all seasoned practitioners with deep learning. Among them was one named Chundian, who, during the sequence of entering the room for instruction, displayed a defiant and unyielding spirit.

He broke through the enclosure and pursued [the Master] all the way to the Dharma Hall, intending to drive him out. The Master resolved the situation, saying, "It is but a common occurrence for Chan practitioners to contend over Chan."
"How could it have come to this? Pò'ān said, "Have you not heard the Way? My stomach is hungry; hearing the sound of the wooden board, I am going to eat.

When the Master heard these words, he could not help but break into a cold sweat that drenched his back. Not long after, he took leave to go to Huázàng, where he relied upon Yǎndùn'ān for three years.
He then returned to Língyǐn, where Pò'ān occupied the position of First Seat (Dìyīzuò). After the midday meal, they went together to visit Shísǔn.
Poyan. A seeker of the Way asked Poyan for further instruction, saying, "I cannot catch this monkey;
I beg the Master for a skillful means. Poyan said, "What is the use of trying to catch it? It is like wind blowing across water; patterns form naturally.
Upon hearing this, the Master’s lifelong sense of obstruction vanished as he departed without a word. Zhang Gongze of Yuozhai, having newly established Guanghui Temple, invited him there.
When Pò'ān founded [the monastery], the Master went with him and attended upon him for three years. When the assembly dispersed, they traveled together to Jìngshān for another three years.
When Pò'ān went to Tiāntóng to pay respects at Mìmǎn’s stupa, he and the Master crossed the Hong River together.

Upon Pò'ān’s departure for Qiónglóng, the Master remained at Tiāntóng, relying on Guān Xī'ān, who appointed him as the director of the repository (guīcángsī); he did not accept. When Pò'ān retired from Qiónglóng, he returned to Jìngshān.
The Master went to visit and pay his respects to Pò’ān Qiānjì. Pò’ān entrusted him with his monastic robe and portrait, but the Master did not accept them;
he accepted only the calligraphic works of Yuànwù and the recorded teachings of Mìmǎn. After the funeral rites were completed, the Master visited his old friend Yúnyúnkō at Qiónglóng.
He served as the head of the assembly for Yúnkō, who was then moving to Ruìguāng Temple. He subsequently held the position of board-head there. Not long after, Quán Gāoyuán...
Siming Lizhou sent a summons to Gaoyuan, saying, "If Chan Master Fan is willing to go, I shall accompany him.
Otherwise, even if it were the inner court of Tuṣita Heaven, I would not go. The Master then went with him. Among the various mountains of Siming, Zhangxi was considered the most sublime;
yet Lizhou was twenty *li* from Zhangxi, and the temple stood on a precipitous peak, cold and desolate.
He arrived at Nak (Falls), a place inhabited by non-humans. Master [Wonhyo] resided upon it for three years as if they were but a single day.

He sustained himself on barely enough hemp, wheat, millet, and beans for his daily meals, yet he never showed the slightest sign of hunger. Later, because the crane from Taishan had not yet arrived, he invited Yaksik of the Stone Stream to join him on a tour to Suwon Mountain (Suyeoksan).
At that time, Ungeo was presiding over the affairs of the monastery and invited him to share the seat of the abbot. One night, he suddenly dreamed of a person in magnificent robes...
Guān held a bundle of *máo* grass and presented it to him. The following day, a special envoy from Qingliang in Mingzhou arrived. The Master, weary of traveling, firmly declined their invitation.
Just then, several monks came to visit, saying that their former monastery was Qingliang, which was secluded, profound, and tranquil, and had been known in antiquity as Little Tiantong.
Its protector was surnamed Máo, whose spiritual manifestations were highly renowned. The Master reflected upon his previous dream.

He then changed his robes and accepted the invitation. Upon entering the monastery, he beheld the so-called temple deity; its attire and appearance were no different from what he had dreamed of in the past.
He ascended the hall to expound the Dharma, offering a single incense stick to Pò'ān (Pò'àn), who had truly resided at Yùwáng Monastery during the time of Jiè'ān (Jiè'ān).
The Master recounted the words from his opening of the hall to Xiuyan, who was struck with wonder and said, "From beginning to end, he is a true master.
Furthermore, this man cannot remain at Qingliang for long. After three years, the various Chan communities of the capital recommended the Master for Jiaoshan;

the Imperial Secretariat issued an edict to dispatch him to Fenghua, but the Master did not go. When the edict was issued a second time, he finally departed. One year later, he was transferred to Xuedou.
After three years, he received an imperial decree to move to Yuyuan Temple. Another three years passed, and after leaving Mount Song and Shaolin, he traveled to Jingshan.

By imperial command, the Master was appointed to fill the vacancy there. Upon arriving at the capital, he had an audience with the Chancellor, Prince Shih Wei. The Prince said, "The abbots of Jingshan in recent times have all been veteran elders who lacked the strength to maintain the monastery;
consequently, the buildings are in a state of extreme decay. I have now invited my Master here not only to preside over the Dharma, but also to restore the temple."
"Renewing and expanding [the temple] was the primary objective. The following year, the temple was destroyed by fire.

Previously, the Master had dreamed that a heroic man bestowed upon him twenty-one bright pearls, not knowing what they signified. When the temple burned, it was on the twenty-first day of the fourth month;
the Master had anticipated this number beforehand. Without changing his countenance or expression, he settled the assembly and continued his religious practice as if nothing had happened.

In the seventh month of that year, there was an imperial decree for him to enter the palace. When the Emperor presided over the Xuzheng Hall to receive him in audience, the Master’s responses were detailed and lucid, causing the Emperor’s countenance to change with admiration.
He was granted a gold-embroidered *saṃghāṭī* robe and was further commanded to ascend the seat at the Ciming Hall.
The Emperor drew aside the curtain to listen. The Emperor remarked to Grand Councilor Chen Gongguiyi, "You have long applied your mind to the inner scriptures."
He presented the essential teachings of the Master to him. Lord Chen submitted a memorial stating that they were concise, clear, and direct, and would be of benefit to the sacred governance.

Thereupon, the Master was granted the title Chan Master Fojian, along with silk fabrics, gold and silver coins, an incense casket, tea, medicinal herbs, and other gifts. Each of the attendant monks was also bestowed with gold and silk in varying amounts.
Furthermore, silver and silk certificates for monastic ordination were issued to assist in the restoration of the monastery. Such was the splendor of his imperial favor and the bounty of his gifts.
Since the Buddha’s illumination of the world, there has never been such a thing. Three years later, the temple was completed; yet after another six years, it was destroyed by fire once more.
The Master remained neither startled nor perturbed, neither slow nor hasty, and thus assistance arrived like clouds from all directions.

From Menghou Gong, the regional inspector of Jinghu, to the two commanderies of Sibao in Shu, as well as from Japan across the sea, all dispatched envoys to present offerings. Within a few years, the temple—
The halls were lofty and magnificent; soaring pavilions and surging palaces appeared as if they were objects within a painted scroll.

Forty *li* from the temple, he built several hundred rooms to receive wandering monks (*yun-shui*). Its halls, palaces, and towers were fully equipped with everything that a monastic community (*cong-lin*) ought to possess.
The Emperor personally inscribed his imperial calligraphy and bestowed upon it the title "Wanyan Zhengxu" (Ten Thousand Years of Continuation).

He granted nine thousand *mu* of prime farmland and decreed that his disciples should manage it according to their seniority. Several hundred paces to the west of Zhengxu, he constructed a hermitage as a repository for sacred relics.

A multi-storied pavilion was erected above it to enshrine the imperial calligraphies bestowed upon him throughout his life. In the eastern and western wings of the spacious chambers, he enshrined the patriarchs.

The Master maintained the ancestral offerings of his previous lives; whenever he encountered his birthday, he would perform the Buddhist rite of feeding the Sangha to assist in the merit for the deceased.

This was because, since the barbarian invaders had breached Sichuan, the Master’s ancestral sacrifices had been cut off. His natural affection was so profound that it could not be untied from his heart.

When the Emperor heard of this, he marveled at him and bestowed upon him the plaque "Yuanzhao" (Perfect Illumination), as detailed in the biography by Official Li Xinzhuan, Director of the Academy of Scholarly Worthies.
It is recorded that Dongxiao is situated between Lin’an and [the capital]. Whenever monastics ascended the mountain, they invariably passed through it on their way.

The city and county were cluttered and chaotic, offering no place for food or rest. There was an old, abandoned temple called Baojin; the Master renovated it, purchased fields, and established a kitchen.

Those who arrived did so as if returning home. At the beginning of the Xiangshu era, the state was established in Qiantang; northern horses gathered there in such numbers that there was nowhere for them to be contained.

Since the region west of Zhejiang borders lakes, the marshlands were used as pastures, and the administration of horse management fell into ruin. Consequently, it was permitted for those with the means to enclose these lands and convert them into fields.

The tax burden on the people was increased by one-third of the cultivated fields. During the Endong era, as court officials petitioned for reform, they noted that many "enclosed fields" (*weitian*) were being concealed;

consequently, the system of land demarcation (*jingjie*) was implemented once again. Even the estates of wealthy and noble families in the capital could not escape this, and a single manor in Guangling belonging to a monastery was entirely designated as an enclosed field.
The Master went to the palace to present his memorial, and by imperial decree, it was granted a special exemption. Although Mount Jing was situated amidst ten thousand mountains...
In the meantime, firewood was insufficient for cooking. Previously, the people had been recruited to enter the mountains to gather firewood;
half of their labor had been exempted as compensation for their service. Consequently, the four surrounding mountains became utterly denuded because of this.

The Master established a thousand *mu* of fields and set up an office to manage them, collecting fees for manual labor and thus relieving the forests from the calamity of constant felling. Furthermore, he planted several million pine and cypress trees to restore them.

Regarding the scenic excellence: in the autumn of the Wushen year of the Chunyou era, the temple was rebuilt. The Master constructed a dwelling by the Mingyue Pond and named it "Retiring from Plowing.

He requested retirement from the court, but his chronic illness coincidentally flared up; it did not subside throughout the spring. On the first day of the third month, he ascended the hall and addressed the assembly, saying:
"This mountain monk is both old and ill; I lack the strength to engage in idle chatter with you all here and there. Today..."
Having completed his studies, he said, "That which I previously failed to exhaustively explain, I shall now shake out before you all.
He then rose and shook his robes, asking, "How much is there? On the fifteenth day, he gathered the two classes of attendants to arrange for his final affairs.
He personally wrote his testament and some dozen letters; his speech and laughter were as harmonious and playful as ever. Someone informed him [of the news].
"This is the great matter at the end; you, Master, should exercise your sovereign authority. The Master said, "The moment one exercises sovereign authority, it is no longer so.
His disciples requested that he leave behind a final verse. The Master smiled and said, "I have not yet looked up the rhymes.
While a physician was examining him, the Master said to him, "You do not recognize that there is still one pulse remaining. At dawn on the eighteenth day, he asked for a brush and wrote:
A verse: When an attendant monk brought paper and brush, the Master said, "What do you say for the first phrase?
The monk replied, "This is the second phrase. Thereupon, the Master took up the brush and wrote swiftly: "Coming, empty and bare; departing, naked and stripped.

If you wish further to inquire into the ultimate point, there is the Stone Bridge at Tiantai. After a short while, he passed away. His coffin remained enshrined for fourteen days. He left behind a memorial table.
I have heard that on the first day of the fourth month, an imperial messenger was dispatched to bestow incense and ceremonial silk.

On the twentieth day, the master’s entire remains were enshrined in a stupa at Yuanzhao, in accordance with his final instructions. The Master’s demeanor was composed and leisurely; his character was broad and expansive.

He was generous without being lax, and discerning without being scrutinizing. He never raised a harsh voice or showed a stern countenance. His followers numbered several hundred, yet he regarded them as if they were...
A passerby remarked: "He dwells uprightly in his small room, possessing no extraordinary objects nor exquisite delicacies; he remains as serene as an ordinary monk.

The people of Wu are fond of giving, and for many years they have brought almsbowls to him no fewer than hundreds of thousands of times. Once these are entrusted to the administrative staff, he does not fuss over them;

he does not calculate the income and expenditure, nor does he even take account of any deficits. Even when encountering great adversity, he remains composed and tranquil, appearing almost unconcerned."
When the temple was burned down for a second time, the Master sat amidst the roar of falling rocks. Several men were carrying his luggage;
halfway along the path, they opened the lock and carried off more than half of it. The Master witnessed this, yet throughout his life he never spoke the names of those individuals.

Once, while making a minor excursion, a servant official neglected his duty, and a strong man carried away what was heavy. Later, when the person was found, the Master’s disciples seized him and interrogated him. The Master—
He replied, "I have no such thing. Although he did not speak further, the raging flames were already fierce, and the crowd was all interrogating him for the name of the one who had set the fire.
When the Master saw this, he hurriedly told them, "If you insist on staying here, flee at once! If the master of the establishment is caught, you will not be treated with such leniency.
To the right of the triple gate, he constructed a multi-storied pavilion; above it, ten thousand Buddha statues were enshrined, and below, the monks' quarters were opened out.
The expenditure amounted to several hundred thousand [coins]. One night, a great wind toppled it. When the Master returned from outside, the assembly thought he would be overcome with grief;
however, the Master said, "Fortunately, it collapsed early. Had it been left for several more years, what if people had been injured beneath it?
His broad-minded benevolence was generally like this. In his youth, he did not take pleasure in study; while living in seclusion, he never once took up a scroll.
When the drum sounded and the assembly gathered, he spoke freely from his mouth; it was often not afflicted by prolixity, nor was it ever afflicted by brevity.
He did not employ perilous rhetoric or strange speech to deceive later students. His style was level and plain yet steep and lofty; concise and clear yet supple and vital.

It was like rolling a ball down a ridge a thousand fathoms high: whether moving forward or backward, ascending or descending, no trace could be found. Seated upon his mat within the meditation hall, his swift wit struck with piercing force.
He was swift; he broke the mountain and cut off the current. As for administering medicine according to the illness, he was able to skillfully apply expedient means. He often said:

"When one joins their palms in greeting, they have already fully recognized where the person comes from. He did not record faults, did not suppress virtues, and would not accept slander. When accused, he did not enforce the law to intimidate the assembly.
For this reason, scholars throughout the world flocked to him like to a marketplace. When the fires of the melting furnace blazed with cruelty, ten thousand tiles were reduced to ash.
Even when flying, though he sat exposed to the elements and slept under the eaves, he could not bear to leave.
Thus, the number of people he attracted was the greatest among all the elders of his time. At another time, the master of Jingshan was the Way-possessing Daohui, the Elder;

yet before ten years had passed, our Master already sat grandly in the abbot’s quarters for nearly twenty years. Harvests were bountiful, and the assembly gathered like the sea, even during two periods of great hardship.

After a period of decline, it has now returned to its former state. How magnificent! Ancient sages have said that when the words and deeds of predecessors are not recorded in biographies, later scholars have no standard upon which to model themselves; this is indeed the fault of the disciples at the time.

Having recently come to Jingshan, I have had the opportunity to attend the Master’s seat. The Master did not disdain my ignorance, and regarding the primary and secondary branches of his family lineage...

The sequence of his stations and the lineage of his teachers and friends have been clearly explained in your instruction. I have humbly listened to these remnants of your wisdom and respectfully wear them upon my person.
Consequently, I have come to understand how Fushan Yuanjian was described by Enxiao and Yingshi, and how Shimen Yun’an was transmitted by Jiyin.
His daily conduct and every movement were recorded without omitting even the finest detail; thus, the significance of the relationship between teacher and student transcended mere ink upon paper.
On an idle day, he compiled his recollections and entrusted them to his attendant scribe, establishing a foundation for future grand inscriptions and deep carvings.

Though this junior student lacks literary refinement and dares not presume to rank among the venerable seniors, the principles of righteousness that reside within the human heart are the same throughout all time and across the world.
This is the second plan.

As for this record, those portions where the old woodblocks have already become blurred and illegible were ordered to be re-engraved by skilled artisans. It is now placed within the Kongo Zen-in at Mount Kiyosumi.
I humbly pray that—

The lineage of the Buddhas shall never be severed. Generation after generation, the banner of radiant light is raised; the ancestral seal is personally transmitted, and every person opens the inexhaustible treasury.
Written on the final summer month of the Gengxu year by the monk Miaopu of the Eastern Hall at Tianlong Temple.
